Upon α-Syn exposure, we detected an increase in mitophagosomes in both cell types (Supplementary Fig. 3b, c). However, Baf A1 treatment further elevated mitophagosome levels only in microglial cells, and not in neuronal cells. A similar phenotype was observed for mitolysosomes (Supplementary Fig. 3e, f), suggesting impaired mitophagy in neuronal cells but preserved or elevated flux in microglia. This is in accordance with our previous observations of impaired autophagy flux in neuronal cells but not in microglia following α-Syn aggregate exposure<sup>42</sup>, consequently affecting mitophagy dynamics.
## α-Syn leads to BAX-mediated mtDNA release

Permeabilization of the outer mitochondrial membrane (MOMP) enables the release of mitochondrial matrix components, including mtDNA, into the cytosol. Having observed MOMP in both neuronal and microglial cells upon α-Syn exposure, we next asked whether this led to mtDNA release. Co-immunostaining for double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) (to label mtDNA) and mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) revealed the presence of both TFAM-negative mtDNA and TFAM-positive nucleoids outside mitochondria (Fig. 3a). Of note, the observed cytosolic DNA particles were negative for DAPI counterstain, thereby excluding a possible role of micronuclei in our study. The proportion of extra-mitochondrial mtDNA increased significantly in both cell types upon α-Syn aggregate exposure (Fig. 3b, c). 3D reconstructions of mtDNA and mitochondrial fluorescence signals further confirmed this, enabling quantification of mtDNA retained within mitochondria (DNA-in) versus released in the cytosol (DNA-out) (Fig. 3d, e). Such events were accompanied by the assembly of activated BAX (6A7) on the mitochondrial membrane (Fig. 3f, g), consistent with reports that BAX macropores facilitate mtDNA efflux<sup>50</sup>. To validate the functional role of BAX in α-Syn aggregate-induced mtDNA release, we pharmacologically inhibited BAX (using BAI-1) and observed a prevention of mtDNA release into the cytoplasm (Fig.3h, i). Together, these results suggest that assembly of activated BAX on mitochondrial membranes provides an escape route for mtDNA upon α-Syn aggregate stress (Fig. 3j).
## α-Syn activates the STING pathway and inflammation

Because of its ancestral prokaryotic origin, mtDNA release into the cytosol can trigger innate immune responses and consequent neuroinflammation. Upon recognition by cytosolic nucleic acid sensors such as cGAS, the second messenger cGAMP is produced, promoting dimerization and Golgi translocation of the ER-resident protein STING, marking its activation<sup>51</sup>. With diABZI, a pharmacological STING agonist, as a positive control, we observed that exposure of both neuronal and microglial cells to α-Syn aggregates, but not monomers, led to a marked increase in STING fluorescence intensity on GM130+ Golgi (Fig. 4a–c and Supplementary Fig. 4a–c). A similar STING-Golgi overlap was observed in iPSC-derived hNeurons and hMG, suggesting a

conserved biological response to α-Syn aggregates in different model systems (Fig. 4d, e, f). Following STING activation, Tank Binding Kinase 1 (TBK1) is recruited to the Golgi compartments and activated via transphosphorylation<sup>52,53</sup>. Consistently, we observed an increase in the number of pTBK1 puncta per cell (Fig. 4g, h, i) and the total area of these particles (Fig. 4j, k), confirming activation of the STING-TBK1 axis.

We next examined whether activation of the STING pathway led to an innate immune response, and whether this response differed between neuronal and microglial cells. Immunostaining for the key pro-inflammatory transcription factors downstream of STING—NF-κB and IRF3—revealed a marked increase in nuclear localization of both total and phosphorylated NF-κB in response to α-Syn aggregates in SH-SY5Y and HMC3 cells (Supplementary Fig. 5a–f). Additionally, we observed no significant translocation of NF-κB to the nuclei of cells exposed to α-Syn monomers, indicative of the inflammatory effects of aggregated forms of the protein (Supplementary Fig. 4d–f). Such an activation of NF-κB was observed in iPSC-derived hNeurons and hMG as well (Supplementary Fig. 5g, h), indicating a conserved response across model systems. Similarly, total and phosphorylated IRF3 showed significantly enhanced nuclear accumulation in both cell types (Supplementary Fig. 5i–n). However, when we assessed downstream gene expression by RT-PCR, microglial cells exhibited a substantially stronger transcriptional response. Expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and phagolysosomal marker (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, CD68; Supplementary Fig. 5o, p) and type I interferons and chemokines (IFNα, IFNβ, CXCL10, CCL20; Supplementary Fig. 5q, r) was consistently and significantly higher in HMC3 compared to SH-SY5Y cells. These results suggest that although both neuronal and microglial cells activate the STING pathway in response to α-Syn, microglia mount a much more robust innate immune response, highlighting their distinct roles in neuroinflammation and disease progression.

To further validate the involvement of mtDNA in triggering an innate immune response, we inhibited its release via BAX inhibition and assessed the translocation of STING to the Golgi and NF-κB to the nuclei. Even in the presence of α-Syn aggregates, BAX-inhibited cells exhibited neither activation of STING (Supplementary Fig. 6a–c) nor nuclear occupancy of NF-κB (Supplementary Fig. 6d–f), thereby strengthening the involvement of BAX-mediated mtDNA release in activation of the STING signaling cascade.
